newsitem.title: JAPAN: YEAREND - Japan metals demand seen flat in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Japan metals demand seen flat in 1997.

text.p: Base metal demand in Japan, the world's second-largest consumer after the United States, will probably be flat next year because of slowing economic growth and a continuing shift in Japanese manufacturing overseas, analysts and industry officials said.
In some sectors, especially aluminium, a rush of consumer buying ahead of next April's consumption tax hike is expected to boost demand temporarily, but the longer-term picture is lacklustre.
"I don't think there'll be a decline in demand, but there's little reason to expect much growth," said one Japanese industry analyst.

UBS Securities Ltd analyst Stephen Wolfe echoed this view. With Japan's economy likely to decelerate next year, he forecast only marginal gains in Japan's demand for non-ferrous metals of about one to two percent.
Economists generally expect Japan's economic growth in the fiscal year from April 1997 to be 1.5 to 2.0 percent, compared with about 2.5 percent in 1996/97.

"Copper offtake will be up one percent at most," Wolfe said, adding that increased demand for copper in power cables is likely to be offset by declining demand in transmission cables, where optical fibres "are eating copper's lunch".
He did not think the air conditioning sector, a heavy user of copper tubing, would see much improvement after this year's record performance.
Wolfe predicted slightly stronger growth in zinc consumption of 1.5 to 2.0 percent, buoyed by rising automobile production and commercial construction.
He doubted, however, that the aluminium sector could sustain the strong growth of this year, when shipments reached record levels as the housing and beverage can sectors boomed.

Data from the Japan Aluminum Federation showed that in the fiscal half-year to September, shipments of flat-rolled and extruded aluminium products were up 4.7 percent from the same period the year before.

A forecast in October by trade house Marubeni concurred with Wolfe's view, predicting that Japan's domestic aluminium demand in the fiscal year from April 1997 would fall 2.3 percent, after rising 3.2 percent in the prior year.

Aluminium demand, especially from the housing sector, was nevertheless expected to remain strong in the January-March quarter of next year, as consumers were seen buying big-ticket items in advance of April's consumption tax hike.
A more bullish outlook on metals demand was advanced by Basil Masters, analyst at Schroder Securities (Japan) Ltd.
He predicted copper demand would grow at least two percent in 1997 as rising industrial activity boosts demand for copper wire and cable.
Schroder bucked the consensus by forecasting an acceleration in Japan's economic growth next year, arguing that a need to boost inventory levels would spur industrial output.
Masters expected Japan's zinc demand would be flat to marginally higher next year, supported by rising automobile production, while lead would be lifted by improved battery consumption.
An official from the Japan Storage Battery Association said, however, that any gains next year from higher automobile output would be offset by a rise in imported batteries.

In the copper market, the Japanese industry analyst predicted cable and wire demand from the construction sector would remain favourable, although overseas shifts of production would limit demand in the car and electric goods sectors.
An expected fall-off in public works spending would also limit copper cable demand from the telecommunications and electric power sectors, he said.

Demand from brassmakers was seen as sluggish, he said, with a drop in air conditioner output, after inventories surged this year, likely to offset a recovery in output of lead frames for semiconductors.
